questions.stem: Two FGCP peers show out-of-sync; only WWAN IPv6 differs and heartbeat counters are healthy. What is safest?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Compare each modem-learned address and document the exception; avoid checksum recalculation.
choices.feedback: The dynamic cellular address explains this documented false-positive checksum mismatch; recalculation can overwrite the peer address.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Force a full resync immediately and clear every checksum difference.
choices.feedback: A force-resync does not identify the checksum eligibility defect and can change unrelated state.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Run checksum recalculation on both members before checking modem state.
choices.feedback: Recalculation is specifically discouraged because the modem-learned address can be overwritten on the peer.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Disable heartbeat monitoring so the dashboard no longer reports drift.
choices.feedback: Disabling monitoring hides genuine failures and does not correct the configuration checksum comparison.

questions.explanation: The dynamic cellular address explains this documented false-positive checksum mismatch; recalculation can overwrite the peer address.

questions.stem: In `get system ha status`, what do healthy HBDEV/MONDEV counters establish during this incident?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They prove every configuration table has matching checksums across both members.
choices.feedback: Configuration equality is reported separately under Configuration Status and its checksum dump.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They show heartbeat and monitored links are passing traffic between cluster members.
choices.feedback: The counters support healthy heartbeat and monitored-interface paths; they do not prove checksum equality.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They confirm the provider assigned identical IPv6 addresses to both cellular modems.
choices.feedback: Each LTE modem can receive a different provider IPv6 address, so equality is not expected.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They demonstrate that every policy and route is synchronized without further checks.
choices.feedback: Policy and route propagation still require separate observation, especially when another table differs.

questions.explanation: The counters support healthy heartbeat and monitored-interface paths; they do not prove checksum equality.

questions.stem: A different non-WWAN table appears after an upgrade and a controlled change fails to propagate. What next?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ignore it because every HA checksum difference is caused by cellular addressing.
choices.feedback: The exception is narrow; other tables need normal HA synchronization troubleshooting.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Recalculate checksums before collecting the table name or member status.
choices.feedback: Recalculation can be destructive in the known case and is not the first diagnostic step.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Treat it as a real mismatch; inspect that table and confirm firmware parity first.
choices.feedback: Non-WWAN differences plus failed propagation are not covered by the documented WWAN exception.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Replace the LTE modem address with the primary member's static IPv6 value.
choices.feedback: Static assignment changes the design and does not establish why the table diverged.

questions.explanation: Non-WWAN differences plus failed propagation are not covered by the documented WWAN exception.

questions.stem: Why should an operator avoid `diagnose ha checksum recalculate` for the documented WWAN mismatch?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It repairs the LTE provider lease but leaves the HA checksum unchanged.
choices.feedback: The warning is about peer address state, not a repair of the provider lease.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It disables the secondary heartbeat interface until the next election.
choices.feedback: The command does not disable HBDEV; heartbeat state is a separate diagnostic.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It converts the dynamic modem address into a synchronized static address.
choices.feedback: The checksum process does not convert the modem lease into a supported static configuration.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It can temporarily overwrite the peer's modem-learned WWAN IPv6 address.
choices.feedback: Fortinet Community explicitly warns that recalculation can overwrite the other unit's WWAN IPv6 address.

questions.explanation: Fortinet Community explicitly warns that recalculation can overwrite the other unit's WWAN IPv6 address.

questions.stem: Before running database integrity checks in workspace mode, which preparation is required?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use one administrator, clear object locks, and unlock all ADOMs.
choices.feedback: The guide requires one logged-in administrator, no locked objects, and unlocked ADOMs in workspace mode.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Keep all ADOM locks active and run checks from several administrators.
choices.feedback: Concurrent administrators and locked objects violate the documented preconditions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Install a policy package first, then check only the affected FortiGate.
choices.feedback: A policy install is not a substitute for database integrity preparation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reboot FortiManager and run the check while workspace locks remain held.
choices.feedback: Rebooting does not remove workspace locks or satisfy the documented check preconditions.

questions.explanation: The guide requires one logged-in administrator, no locked objects, and unlocked ADOMs in workspace mode.

questions.stem: `diagnose pm2 check-integrity all` reports malformed ADOM data. What does this command do?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It restores every malformed ADOM from the latest revision history.
choices.feedback: ADOM revision history is not a physical database repair mechanism.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It detects database integrity errors but does not repair corrupted records.
choices.feedback: The upgrade guide states the integrity check detects errors; it cannot correct them.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It rebuilds SQLite indexes automatically and resumes policy installation.
choices.feedback: The command reports the fault rather than rebuilding damaged SQLite structures.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It converts the ADOM database into the global database recovery target.
choices.feedback: ADOM and global databases have separate recovery scopes; this command does not convert them.

questions.explanation: The upgrade guide states the integrity check detects errors; it cannot correct them.

questions.stem: Which evidence best verifies a FortiManager system backup before attempting recovery?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Confirm the backup dialog closed and assume the file is complete.
choices.feedback: A closed dialog proves the operation ended, not that the backup file is intact.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Check that Policy & Objects opens once, then delete older backups.
choices.feedback: A single GUI view does not validate the recovery artifact or justify deleting backups.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Compare the backup file's checksum with the MD5 recorded in System Event Log.
choices.feedback: The guide directs administrators to compare the event-log MD5 with the saved backup file.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Compare the FortiGate policy-package checksum with the FortiManager backup name.
choices.feedback: Policy-package checksums are unrelated to the system backup file's integrity.

questions.explanation: The guide directs administrators to compare the event-log MD5 with the saved backup file.

questions.stem: The Community article reports an ADOM recovery command in 7.6.10. What is safest before using it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Run the global database recovery command because all SQLite files share one scope.
choices.feedback: Global recovery is documented for the global database, not as generic ADOM repair.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Execute the community command on 7.6.7 before checking the database type.
choices.feedback: The reported command is tied to a later build; running it on 7.6.7 is unsupported.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Restore a policy revision and assume the physical database has been repaired.
choices.feedback: Policy revisions do not repair malformed SQLite pages or missing index rows.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Verify the installed build and TAC guidance, then preserve a known-good backup.
choices.feedback: The command is Community-reported and not independently confirmed in the official CLI reference; protect the backup first.

questions.explanation: The command is Community-reported and not independently confirmed in the official CLI reference; protect the backup first.

questions.stem: Which prerequisites are required before FortiAnalyzer can deliver blocked indicators through FortiMQ?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Shared FortiCare registration, FortiGate logging, and Cloud-based Fabric Feed synchronization.
choices.feedback: FortiMQ requires FortiAnalyzer/FortiGate under the same FortiCare account and a synchronized FortiGate feed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A FortiManager license, a custom connector object, and a global ADOM policy.
choices.feedback: FortiMQ is built into the ADOM; it does not require a custom connector object.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A FortiGate local address object, an API token, and an SSL-VPN tunnel.
choices.feedback: Local address objects and SSL-VPN do not establish the FortiMQ feed path.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An event handler, a report schedule, and an external syslog receiver.
choices.feedback: Event handlers and reports detect activity; they do not satisfy the connector prerequisites.

questions.explanation: FortiMQ requires FortiAnalyzer/FortiGate under the same FortiCare account and a synchronized FortiGate feed.

questions.stem: What transaction occurs after an analyst selects Block on an indicator in FortiAnalyzer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: FortiAnalyzer immediately installs a deny policy on every managed FortiGate.
choices.feedback: FortiAnalyzer does not directly install firewall policies as part of this connector action.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The `block_indicator` playbook sends the indicator through the enabled FortiMQ connector.
choices.feedback: The documented action runs `block_indicator` in the background and sends the indicator to FortiMQ.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The ADOM automatically creates a new FortiManager package and schedules deployment.
choices.feedback: FortiMQ distribution is separate from FortiManager package installation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The indicator is stored only in the report database until a manual export.
choices.feedback: The indicator is sent to the cloud broker rather than remaining only in a report.

questions.explanation: The documented action runs `block_indicator` in the background and sends the indicator to FortiMQ.

questions.stem: A FortiGate external feed contains the blocked IP, but traffic still passes. What should be checked next?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Recreate the indicator because a feed object always enforces automatically.
choices.feedback: The feed object alone does not create a deny rule or policy match.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Disable FortiMQ and assume FortiManager will install a deny rule.
choices.feedback: Changing connector priority does not create an enforcement reference.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Verify that a firewall policy or security profile references the feed and matches traffic.
choices.feedback: Feed retrieval supplies data; a referencing policy or profile performs enforcement.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Change the FortiCare account because feed visibility proves registration failed.
choices.feedback: A visible feed suggests the account path is working; check the policy/profile attachment.

questions.explanation: Feed retrieval supplies data; a referencing policy or profile performs enforcement.

questions.stem: How does FortiMQ behave when both FortiMQ and FortiManager connectors are enabled?

choices.label: A
choices.text: FortiManager always takes priority and distributes indicators globally across ADOMs.
choices.feedback: FortiManager does not retain priority when FortiMQ is enabled.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both connectors always receive every indicator and merge their block lists.
choices.feedback: The guide describes fallback behavior, not simultaneous guaranteed delivery.

choices.label: C
choices.text: FortiMQ applies indicators to every FortiGate registered to the FortiCare account.
choices.feedback: FortiCare registration is necessary but does not remove ADOM scoping.

choices.label: D
choices.text: FortiMQ takes priority and applies indicators only within the current ADOM.
choices.feedback: The guide states FortiMQ has priority and is ADOM-specific; FortiManager is used when FortiMQ is disabled.

questions.explanation: The guide states FortiMQ has priority and is ADOM-specific; FortiManager is used when FortiMQ is disabled.

questions.stem: On FortiSwitchOS 8.0, what does `set protocol dot` change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It moves the switch's own system DNS client to TLS over TCP port 853.
choices.feedback: DoT protects switch-originated DNS queries and responses on TCP/853.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It encrypts all endpoint DNS packets that traverse every access switch port.
choices.feedback: Transit endpoint DNS is not automatically intercepted or encrypted by this system DNS setting.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It changes the management GUI to use HTTPS on TCP port 853.
choices.feedback: The management GUI protocol and port are unrelated to system DNS transport.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It tunnels DHCP option requests through the switch's DNS resolver.
choices.feedback: DHCP option processing is not part of the switch's DNS client.

questions.explanation: DoT protects switch-originated DNS queries and responses on TCP/853.

questions.stem: What security property is added when `server-ca-cert` is configured for the DoT resolver?

choices.label: A
choices.text: FortiSwitch encrypts DNS names without validating the resolver's identity.
choices.feedback: Without a CA certificate, DoT still encrypts but does not perform this CA validation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: FortiSwitch validates the resolver certificate chain before establishing TLS.
choices.feedback: The guide states that a configured CA certificate is used for certificate validation before connection.

choices.label: C
choices.text: FortiSwitch signs each DNS response using its local administrator password.
choices.feedback: The local administrator password is not a DNS response-signing key.

choices.label: D
choices.text: FortiSwitch changes the resolver's TCP port from 853 to 53.
choices.feedback: DoT uses TCP/853; it does not switch back to port 53.

questions.explanation: The guide states that a configured CA certificate is used for certificate validation before connection.

questions.stem: A capture shows a successful TCP/853 handshake, but the switch cannot resolve an internal name. What next?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increase the access VLAN MTU and clear all learned MAC addresses.
choices.feedback: MTU and MAC learning are not the first checks for a switch-originated DNS lookup.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Disable DoT permanently because TCP reachability proves the resolver is incompatible.
choices.feedback: Reachability does not prove incompatibility; inspect TLS and DNS response behavior.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Check resolver routing, source IP, certificate trust, and the DNS answer itself.
choices.feedback: A TCP handshake proves reachability only; trust, source selection, and DNS data remain separate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Change the switch management HTTPS certificate and retry the same lookup.
choices.feedback: The management GUI certificate is unrelated to the upstream resolver certificate.

questions.explanation: A TCP handshake proves reachability only; trust, source selection, and DNS data remain separate.

questions.stem: Why can endpoint DNS traffic still appear on UDP/53 after enabling FortiSwitch DoT?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The switch falls back to UDP/53 for every client by design.
choices.feedback: There is no documented universal fallback of client DNS to UDP/53.

choices.label: B
choices.text: DoT encrypts only DNS replies, while endpoint requests remain in plaintext.
choices.feedback: DoT encapsulates the switch's queries and responses; it does not split request encryption.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The resolver's certificate disables encryption for devices behind the switch.
choices.feedback: Resolver certificate validation does not control endpoint packet encryption.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The setting protects the switch's system DNS client, not transit endpoint queries.
choices.feedback: The documented feature changes the FortiSwitch system DNS client, not transit traffic.

questions.explanation: The documented feature changes the FortiSwitch system DNS client, not transit traffic.

questions.stem: Which statement about the FAP-441K and FAP-443K MLO radio matrix is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Their 5 and 6 GHz radios support MLO, but 2.4 GHz does not.
choices.feedback: The guide states that 441K and 443K lack Wi-Fi 7 MLO on 2.4 GHz.

choices.label: B
choices.text: All three radios support MLO when the controller runs FortiOS 8.0.
choices.feedback: The model matrix is radio-specific; a 8.0 controller cannot add unsupported hardware capability.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only the 2.4 GHz radio supports MLO on those K-series models.
choices.feedback: The guide identifies 5 and 6 GHz support, not 2.4 GHz.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Those models require a separate SSID for each MLO radio link.
choices.feedback: MLO uses a multi-link VAP rather than requiring one SSID per link.

questions.explanation: The guide states that 441K and 443K lack Wi-Fi 7 MLO on 2.4 GHz.

questions.stem: A WPA3-SAE VAP has MLO enabled but is not applied to the intended AP radios. What is missing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enable WPA2 transition mode and let each radio inherit a separate VAP.
choices.feedback: WPA2 transition mode is not the documented MLO security prerequisite.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Map the VAP into the intended radio sections of the WTP profile.
choices.feedback: The VAP must be assigned to the intended radios through the WTP profile.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Change the controller heartbeat interval and restart the FortiGate cluster.
choices.feedback: Controller heartbeat does not assign the VAP to radio interfaces.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create a second SSID for every frequency band and disable MLO.
choices.feedback: The guide uses one VAP mapped to selected radios, not separate SSIDs.

questions.explanation: The VAP must be assigned to the intended radios through the WTP profile.

questions.stem: Which additional settings are required for MLO on a local standalone bridge-mode SSID?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enable tunnel mode, remote RADIUS, and central DHCP relay on the VAP.
choices.feedback: Those are centrally managed tunnel-mode dependencies, not the standalone MLO prerequisites.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enable mesh backhaul, rogue AP suppression, and dynamic VLAN assignment.
choices.feedback: Mesh, rogue AP and VLAN settings do not establish standalone local authentication.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enable local-standalone, local-bridging, and local-authentication on the VAP.
choices.feedback: The guide lists these three local settings for standalone MLO operation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enable controller discovery, CAPWAP encryption, and FortiManager workspace mode.
choices.feedback: CAPWAP and FortiManager workspace settings are unrelated to the standalone VAP requirements.

questions.explanation: The guide lists these three local settings for standalone MLO operation.

questions.stem: Which evidence proves that a client actually established multiple MLO links?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The SSID appears in the client scan list on both 5 and 6 GHz.
choices.feedback: SSID visibility proves advertisement, not multi-link association.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The FortiGate dashboard shows the AP online with all radios enabled.
choices.feedback: An online AP and enabled radios do not prove client MLO negotiation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The client receives an IP address from the expected DHCP scope.
choices.feedback: DHCP success proves IP connectivity, not the number of 802.11 links.

choices.label: D
choices.text: `diagnose wpa wpad mld` shows multiple link IDs and a `num_links` value above one.
choices.feedback: The MLD diagnostic exposes link count and link IDs for the associated client.

questions.explanation: The MLD diagnostic exposes link count and link IDs for the associated client.

questions.stem: What does FortiNAC require for PEAP/MSCHAPv2 against Active Directory?

choices.label: A
choices.text: FortiNAC must join the domain and use Winbind for the supported AD authentication path.
choices.feedback: PEAP/MSCHAPv2 is AD-only, requires domain membership, and uses Winbind.

choices.label: B
choices.text: FortiNAC must use local guest accounts and disable the server certificate.
choices.feedback: Local guest users are associated with TTLS/PAP, not this AD-only method.

choices.label: C
choices.text: FortiNAC must use EAP-TLS with an endpoint trust certificate for every user.
choices.feedback: EAP-TLS is a different method that authenticates with client certificates.

choices.label: D
choices.text: FortiNAC must query multiple AD domains through an LDAP proxy.
choices.feedback: The documented PEAP/MSCHAPv2 configuration is limited to one domain.

questions.explanation: PEAP/MSCHAPv2 is AD-only, requires domain membership, and uses Winbind.

questions.stem: After KB5127648, cached PEAP credentials fail with Event ID 12014, but manual credentials succeed. What is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: FortiNAC lost its RADIUS shared secret during the Windows update.
choices.feedback: A manual success does not support a general shared-secret failure.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Windows cached-credential NTLMv1 SSO behavior changed on the endpoint.
choices.feedback: The Community tip ties the symptom to cached SSO behavior and the Windows update.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The access switch stopped forwarding EAPOL frames to the RADIUS server.
choices.feedback: The same endpoint's manual authentication makes a basic EAPOL forwarding failure less likely.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The FortiNAC server certificate expired at the same time as the update.
choices.feedback: Certificate expiry would usually affect the outer TLS path, not only cached credentials.

questions.explanation: The Community tip ties the symptom to cached SSO behavior and the Windows update.

questions.stem: Which observation most strongly separates the Windows cached-credential issue from a FortiNAC RADIUS defect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every EAP method fails from every client on the same access switch.
choices.feedback: A failure across every method points toward a broader service or network fault.

choices.label: B
choices.text: FortiNAC cannot reach any domain controller from the management network.
choices.feedback: Domain-controller reachability is a separate dependency and would affect more than cached SSO.

choices.label: C
choices.text: EAP-TLS and manual PEAP credentials work while automatic Windows logon credentials fail.
choices.feedback: That pattern isolates the cached username/password path and leaves other authentication paths working.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The RADIUS server stops receiving Access-Requests from all NAS devices.
choices.feedback: No Access-Requests would indicate transport or NAS configuration, not this endpoint-specific behavior.

questions.explanation: That pattern isolates the cached username/password path and leaves other authentication paths working.

questions.stem: What is the safest long-term direction after using the documented BlockNtlmv1SSO workaround?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Leave the NTLMv1 SSO control weakened permanently on every Windows endpoint.
choices.feedback: Permanent weakening expands the exposure and is not a durable authentication design.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Disable PEAP server-certificate validation to avoid future cached credential failures.
choices.feedback: Outer TLS certificate validation is not the cause identified by the article.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Replace all local RADIUS settings with an unauthenticated guest VLAN.
choices.feedback: An unauthenticated guest VLAN removes the required enterprise identity control.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Manage a temporary exception centrally, then migrate affected clients toward EAP-TLS.
choices.feedback: The article's Audit-mode workaround is temporary; certificate-based EAP-TLS avoids this cached-password path.

questions.explanation: The article's Audit-mode workaround is temporary; certificate-based EAP-TLS avoids this cached-password path.

questions.stem: What efficiency improvement does the Microsoft NAC-API provide to FortiNAC-F Intune integration?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It retrieves data for a single discovered host instead of downloading the full asset list.
choices.feedback: The guide describes per-host lookup and avoids repeated full-list retrieval for larger environments.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It disables all polling and imports only devices manually registered by administrators.
choices.feedback: The integration still uses polling/lookup; it does not disable MDM collection.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It replaces Microsoft Graph with local MAC learning from the access switch.
choices.feedback: Local switch MAC learning is not the Microsoft Intune device-data API.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It retrieves compliance status only after every Intune device is exported to CSV.
choices.feedback: CSV export is not the documented NAC-API on-demand workflow.

questions.explanation: The guide describes per-host lookup and avoids repeated full-list retrieval for larger environments.

questions.stem: MSInTuneServer logs show a device was discovered, but Host View has no registered record. `validmac` returns Invalid. What next?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Change the Intune tenant ID and recreate every application permission.
choices.feedback: Tenant changes are not indicated when the poller already discovered the device.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Update Vendor OUI definitions through Auto Definition Sync, then poll again.
choices.feedback: The Community tip identifies a stale Vendor OUI database and prescribes Auto Definition Sync.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Disable MAC validation so any discovered address becomes a registered host.
choices.feedback: Disabling validation removes a registration gate instead of correcting the database.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Replace the host's serial number with the Intune Device ID manually.
choices.feedback: The Device ID and serial number are separate identity fields and should not be overwritten.

questions.explanation: The Community tip identifies a stale Vendor OUI database and prescribes Auto Definition Sync.

questions.stem: Why are Application Permissions preferred for the NAC-API daemon workflow?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They force every device to use the same randomized wireless MAC address.
choices.feedback: MAC randomization is an endpoint identity condition, not an application permission feature.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They remove the need for tenant and client application registration.
choices.feedback: Tenant and client registration remain required integration configuration.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They allow background service access without relying on a delegated signed-in user.
choices.feedback: Application permissions support daemon/background access and single-host API lookup.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They replace certificate or secret authentication with an anonymous API call.
choices.feedback: The API still authenticates the application; anonymous access is not implied.

questions.explanation: Application permissions support daemon/background access and single-host API lookup.

questions.stem: A device registers successfully, but its compliance Boolean is absent. Which area should be examined?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Refresh the Vendor OUI database again because it stores compliance results.
choices.feedback: Vendor OUI maps MAC prefixes to manufacturers and does not hold compliance state.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Change the WTP profile because Intune attributes arrive through wireless radio mapping.
choices.feedback: WTP profiles do not control Microsoft Intune API attributes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rebuild the FortiNAC host database because serial numbers cannot be stored.
choices.feedback: The guide includes serial number and compliance Boolean as separate host fields.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inspect NAC-API permissions and compliance retrieval configuration, not Vendor OUI.
choices.feedback: OUI validation gates MAC registration; compliance data comes from the MDM/API retrieval path.

questions.explanation: OUI validation gates MAC registration; compliance data comes from the MDM/API retrieval path.

questions.stem: What did FortiAuthenticator 8.0.2 add to separate management and HA control traffic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A dedicated Heartbeat Interface separate from the Management interface.
choices.feedback: The 8.0.2 change decouples HA synchronization/health monitoring from management access.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A second RADIUS service port shared by both cluster members.
choices.feedback: RADIUS service ports are separate from the HA interface naming change.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A new VLAN tag for all administrator and user authentication traffic.
choices.feedback: The new setting is an HA heartbeat interface, not a user VLAN tag.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A replacement IPsec tunnel for every remote authentication server.
choices.feedback: Remote authentication tunnels are not replaced by the dedicated heartbeat setting.

questions.explanation: The 8.0.2 change decouples HA synchronization/health monitoring from management access.

questions.stem: What are the documented default heartbeat interval and lost threshold?

choices.label: A
choices.text: One hundred milliseconds between heartbeats and one thousand milliseconds before failover detection.
choices.feedback: The documented defaults are longer than these proposed values.

choices.label: B
choices.text: One thousand milliseconds between heartbeats and six thousand milliseconds before failover detection.
choices.feedback: The guide gives 1000 ms interval and 6000 ms consecutive-heartbeat lost threshold.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Six thousand milliseconds between heartbeats and one thousand milliseconds before failover detection.
choices.feedback: The interval and lost threshold are reversed in this option.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ten seconds between heartbeats and sixty seconds before failover detection.
choices.feedback: The guide does not specify ten- and sixty-second defaults.

questions.explanation: The guide gives 1000 ms interval and 6000 ms consecutive-heartbeat lost threshold.

questions.stem: The administrator cannot reach a Management IP, but cluster members remain in sync. What should be checked first?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The heartbeat lost threshold, because GUI access uses heartbeat packets.
choices.feedback: Heartbeat monitoring is not the administrator GUI path after the 8.0.2 separation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The RADIUS shared secret, because it determines the management IP route.
choices.feedback: RADIUS shared secrets do not control management-plane routing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Management routing, access controls, and node-specific gateway independently of heartbeat.
choices.feedback: The management and heartbeat paths are separate; a management route failure need not break HA.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The load-balancer DNS record, because active-passive HA requires round-robin DNS.
choices.feedback: Round-robin DNS is not a prerequisite for active-passive cluster management.

questions.explanation: The management and heartbeat paths are separate; a management route failure need not break HA.

questions.stem: Why might a node-specific default gateway be required for the HA management interface?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The heartbeat interface always inherits a different gateway from the primary.
choices.feedback: The setting is specifically for management routing, not the heartbeat interface.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The cluster synchronizes management routes only after a RADIUS Access-Accept.
choices.feedback: RADIUS authentication does not trigger management-route synchronization.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The default gateway is automatically copied to every node during election.
choices.feedback: The guide states the node-specific gateway is not replicated.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The management port can use a different gateway that is not replicated to the peer.
choices.feedback: The guide describes a node-specific gateway when the HA management port uses a different route.

questions.explanation: The guide describes a node-specific gateway when the HA management port uses a different route.

questions.stem: What security property does RADIUS Message-Authenticator attribute 80 provide?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It validates packet integrity using the shared secret; it does not encrypt the packet.
choices.feedback: Attribute 80 provides an integrity/authenticity check calculated with the shared secret.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It encrypts every RADIUS attribute and hides the entire UDP payload.
choices.feedback: RADIUS Message-Authenticator is not full-packet encryption.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It replaces the shared secret with a certificate-based TLS handshake.
choices.feedback: It does not replace the RADIUS shared secret with TLS.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It proves that a RADIUS response came from the network access switch.
choices.feedback: The response is validated against the shared secret, not a switch identity assertion.

questions.explanation: Attribute 80 provides an integrity/authenticity check calculated with the shared secret.

questions.stem: What is the FortiPAM 1.9 default for `require-message-authenticator`?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is disabled, allowing responses without attribute 80 by default.
choices.feedback: The documented default is enabled, not disabled.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is enabled, making response Message-Authenticator validation mandatory.
choices.feedback: The release adds the option and enables it by default for response validation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is enabled only for local users and ignored for remote RADIUS users.
choices.feedback: The setting is under the remote RADIUS server object, not only local users.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is automatically enabled only after a failed authentication attempt.
choices.feedback: It is a default configuration behavior, not a failure-triggered change.

questions.explanation: The release adds the option and enables it by default for response validation.

questions.stem: The remote RADIUS server omits attribute 80 in its response. What is the safest remediation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Disable validation permanently across all RADIUS servers and administrator groups.
choices.feedback: Permanent disable removes the security check beyond the affected interoperability case.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Change the FortiPAM user password and leave the response packet unchanged.
choices.feedback: Changing a user password does not add Message-Authenticator to a response.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fix server support first; disable validation only as a documented temporary exception.
choices.feedback: The guide permits disable as a workaround, but restoring server support preserves integrity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Open UDP/1812 publicly so the missing attribute can be retransmitted.
choices.feedback: Opening the port does not make the server calculate attribute 80.

questions.explanation: The guide permits disable as a workaround, but restoring server support preserves integrity.

questions.stem: The RADIUS server logs Access-Accept, but FortiPAM rejects the login. Which evidence is most useful?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Check only UDP reachability and assume the response integrity is valid.
choices.feedback: UDP reachability proves transport only, not attribute validation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inspect the FortiPAM local-user password and reset the administrator account.
choices.feedback: The issue is in the remote RADIUS response path, not a local-user password.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Check the switch's DHCP lease and VLAN assignment for the FortiPAM appliance.
choices.feedback: DHCP/VLAN state may affect reachability but does not validate attribute 80.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Capture attribute 80 in both directions and verify the shared secret on both sides.
choices.feedback: Server acceptance is not proof that FortiPAM accepted the response authenticator.

questions.explanation: Server acceptance is not proof that FortiPAM accepted the response authenticator.

questions.stem: During normal Collector HA operation, which node owns the log-source VIP?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Leader Collector owns the VIP while Supervisor distributes polling and monitoring jobs.
choices.feedback: The Cluster Config guide states the Leader owns the VIP and Supervisor distributes jobs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Supervisor owns the VIP while all Collectors remain passive log relays.
choices.feedback: The Supervisor coordinates jobs; it is not the Collector VIP owner.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The highest-EPS Collector owns the VIP and assigns jobs to the Supervisor.
choices.feedback: Capacity does not elect the Leader based on EPS alone.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The App Server owns the VIP and sends logs to the Leader through HTTP.
choices.feedback: The App Server redistributes jobs; it does not own the Collector VIP.

questions.explanation: The Cluster Config guide states the Leader owns the VIP and Supervisor distributes jobs.

questions.stem: What should happen when the Leader Collector fails in an on-premises VRRP cluster?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Supervisor takes the VIP and permanently disables every Follower Collector.
choices.feedback: The Supervisor is not the VRRP Collector role.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The highest-priority Follower becomes Leader, takes the VIP, and receives redistributed jobs.
choices.feedback: VRRP moves the VIP to the highest-priority Follower and jobs are redistributed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The failed Leader keeps the VIP while the Follower only receives new SNMP jobs.
choices.feedback: The failed Leader cannot keep the VIP after successful failover.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The App Server becomes the new Leader and replaces the Supervisor database.
choices.feedback: The App Server handles job redistribution; it does not replace the Supervisor database.

questions.explanation: VRRP moves the VIP to the highest-priority Follower and jobs are redistributed.

questions.stem: A Follower Collector fails while the Leader remains healthy. What is expected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The VIP moves to the Supervisor while the Leader stops receiving syslog.
choices.feedback: The Supervisor is not the log-source VIP endpoint.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The highest-priority Follower becomes Leader even though the current Leader is healthy.
choices.feedback: Leader election is not triggered by a single Follower loss.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The VIP stays with the Leader while App Server redistributes the failed Follower's jobs.
choices.feedback: A Follower does not own the VIP; job redistribution is the primary response.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The failed Follower continues polling until a manual failover command is issued.
choices.feedback: The App Server redistributes jobs automatically rather than waiting for a manual command.

questions.explanation: A Follower does not own the VIP; job redistribution is the primary response.

questions.stem: Which Collector HA method is documented for Azure and GCP deployments?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use VRRP only; cloud load balancers are reserved for on-premises clusters.
choices.feedback: VRRP is not the documented Azure/GCP design.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Use DNS round-robin only; neither VRRP nor a load balancer is supported.
choices.feedback: DNS round-robin does not provide the documented Collector HA health handling.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use a FortiGate active-passive cluster to replace all Collector nodes.
choices.feedback: FortiGate HA does not replace FortiSIEM Collector clustering.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Use a cloud load balancer; VRRP is documented for on-premises and AWS.
choices.feedback: The architecture guide specifies load balancers for Azure/GCP and VRRP for on-prem/AWS.

questions.explanation: The architecture guide specifies load balancers for Azure/GCP and VRRP for on-prem/AWS.

questions.stem: How are the simplified pre-logon machine-certificate filters evaluated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both the certificate Common Name and Issuer must match the configured filters.
choices.feedback: The documented matching condition uses CN and Issuer together as an AND requirement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Either Common Name or Issuer can match, with the other ignored.
choices.feedback: An either/or match can select a certificate that does not meet policy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only the certificate serial number is checked before connecting to the PoP.
choices.feedback: The feature uses configured identity filters, not serial number alone.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The endpoint selects the newest certificate regardless of issuer or subject.
choices.feedback: Certificate age does not override the configured CN/Issuer checks.

questions.explanation: The documented matching condition uses CN and Issuer together as an AND requirement.

questions.stem: What happens to the pre-logon tunnel when the Windows user signs in?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It remains active and becomes the user's Cloud Security tunnel automatically.
choices.feedback: The machine tunnel is not simply retained as the user tunnel.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It disconnects, then the endpoint follows the configured Cloud Security tunnel behavior.
choices.feedback: The guide describes a disconnect followed by automatic or manual user-tunnel selection.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It changes its machine certificate to the user's password without reconnecting.
choices.feedback: Certificate identity does not change into a password-based session.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It transfers its IPsec security association to the FortiGate gateway.
choices.feedback: The simplified flow connects directly to a FortiSASE PoP, not a customer gateway.

questions.explanation: The guide describes a disconnect followed by automatic or manual user-tunnel selection.

questions.stem: A PoP reports a successful connection attempt, but FortiClient never shows Connected. What conclusion is justified?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The PoP message proves the machine tunnel is fully established and healthy.
choices.feedback: The thread describes a termination after the PoP response, not a completed client state.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The support case proves an intermediate CA certificate is always unsupported.
choices.feedback: The case did not establish a universal intermediate-CA defect.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The endpoint lifecycle is incomplete; inspect certificate selection, allowed destinations, and client logs.
choices.feedback: A PoP-side message is not end-to-end proof; the Community case remained unresolved.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The user's password must be wrong because the machine certificate was accepted.
choices.feedback: Machine-certificate pre-logon occurs before the user password is entered.

questions.explanation: A PoP-side message is not end-to-end proof; the Community case remained unresolved.

questions.stem: Why must at least one FQDN or subnet be configured for simplified pre-logon?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It selects which certificate authority signs the FortiClient user certificate.
choices.feedback: Certificate trust is configured separately from destination policy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It determines the FortiSASE PoP region from the endpoint's DNS suffix.
choices.feedback: PoP selection is based on service proximity, not the allowed destination list alone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It assigns a permanent user VLAN to the machine before login.
choices.feedback: The pre-logon tunnel is a machine-access path, not a VLAN assignment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It defines the corporate destinations reachable through the machine-authenticated tunnel.
choices.feedback: The guide requires an allowed destination so the pre-logon tunnel has a defined access scope.

questions.explanation: The guide requires an allowed destination so the pre-logon tunnel has a defined access scope.

questions.stem: What entitlement must be present for a FortiGate to participate in OaaS provisioning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The required SWOS subscription must cover every participating FortiGate, including spokes.
choices.feedback: The OaaS documentation requires SWOS entitlement on each participating device.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only the primary hub needs a license because spokes inherit its subscription.
choices.feedback: The spokes do not inherit a hub's per-device subscription.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A FortiManager ADOM license replaces the OaaS subscription for all devices.
choices.feedback: FortiManager ADOM licensing is not the OaaS entitlement.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An ADVPN shortcut license is required only on the active spoke.
choices.feedback: ADVPN path discovery is a data-plane feature, not the OaaS subscription.

questions.explanation: The OaaS documentation requires SWOS entitlement on each participating device.

questions.stem: FGFM is healthy, but IPsec overlay tunnels do not establish. What does this indicate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The overlay data plane must be healthy because FGFM uses the same tunnel.
choices.feedback: FGFM and IPsec are different control/data-plane paths.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The management control path works; validate UDP 500/4500, NAT-T, and overlay configuration separately.
choices.feedback: FGFM carries OaaS management transactions; IPsec underlay reachability is a separate path.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The OaaS portal has committed every BGP route and SD-WAN policy successfully.
choices.feedback: A working management tunnel does not prove BGP routes or SD-WAN policies are active.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The FortiGate license is valid because FGFM established a management session.
choices.feedback: License state must be checked directly; FGFM reachability is not license proof.

questions.explanation: FGFM carries OaaS management transactions; IPsec underlay reachability is a separate path.

questions.stem: An OaaS configuration task fails during application. What should the operator expect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The device keeps every successful command and silently skips the failed step.
choices.feedback: Partial commits are not the documented OaaS transaction behavior.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The portal installs a FortiManager revision and reboots all spokes automatically.
choices.feedback: OaaS is not a FortiManager policy-package revision workflow.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The orchestrated change set rolls back, and `get oaas status` exposes task error details.
choices.feedback: The feature applies configuration as a transaction and rolls back the orchestrated changes on failure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The ADVPN hub deletes every shortcut until the next license renewal.
choices.feedback: Shortcut formation is separate from the configuration transaction.

questions.explanation: The feature applies configuration as a transaction and rolls back the orchestrated changes on failure.

questions.stem: What does ADVPN contribute after OaaS provisions the hub-and-spoke overlay?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The FortiCloud portal forwards all branch traffic through its management tunnel.
choices.feedback: FGFM is the management channel, not the user data path.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The FGFM agent encrypts user traffic between spokes over TCP/541.
choices.feedback: TCP/541 is not the ADVPN shortcut transport.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The SWOS subscription creates a static route between every spoke pair.
choices.feedback: Entitlement enables service participation but does not create static routes between every spoke.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The hub informs spokes about better paths so direct spoke shortcuts can form.
choices.feedback: ADVPN shortcut discovery is the data-plane behavior that can bypass the hub for inter-spoke traffic.

questions.explanation: ADVPN shortcut discovery is the data-plane behavior that can bypass the hub for inter-spoke traffic.

questions.stem: Why is `diagnose pm2 db-recover global` not a generic repair for a corrupted ADOM database?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It targets the global database and requires its own offline recovery procedure.
choices.feedback: The documented command is scoped to the global database and is not ADOM recovery.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It repairs every ADOM but only when workspace mode is enabled.
choices.feedback: Workspace mode is a precondition for integrity checks, not a scope conversion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It rebuilds FortiGate policy packages without touching SQLite files.
choices.feedback: Policy package rebuilding does not repair physical database corruption.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It verifies the backup MD5 and automatically restores the ADOM revision.
choices.feedback: Backup verification is separate from the global database recovery command.

questions.explanation: The documented command is scoped to the global database and is not ADOM recovery.

questions.stem: Which observation alone is insufficient to declare the cellular FGCP pair healthy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Matching firmware versions and healthy HBDEV/MONDEV counters on both peers.
choices.feedback: These checks support cluster health when correlated with the WWAN-specific checksum difference.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Different WWAN IPv6 addresses, without checking heartbeat and other configuration tables.
choices.feedback: Different modem-learned addresses are the known checksum trigger, but other health evidence is still required.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Successful controlled configuration propagation after the primary change.
choices.feedback: Successful propagation is useful evidence that ordinary synchronization still works.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Matching non-WWAN configuration checksums and stable monitored interfaces.
choices.feedback: Matching other tables and healthy links support the documented exception diagnosis.

questions.explanation: Different modem-learned addresses are the known checksum trigger, but other health evidence is still required.
